newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-Australian gold sales hurt refiners.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Australian gold sales hurt refiners.

text.p: Australia's largest gold refiner has criticised the Australian central bank for selling two-thirds of the bank's gold reserves and said its refinery business would suffer as a consequence.

"Obviously it hurts us through refining," Don Mackay-Coghill, chief executive officer of GoldCorp, which runs the Australian Gold Refineries and the Perth Mint, told Reuters in an interview on Friday.

Australia's leading politicians have infuriated the gold industry by blaming gold's plunge to 12-year price lows on "screen jockeys" rather than its decision to unload 167 tonnes of gold out of total reserves of 247 tonnes to buy foreign currency-backed currencies.
Gold miners have responded angrily to the sales, with Australia's most successful prospector, multi-millionaire Joseph Gutnick calling on the bank to buy the gold back.

The Gold Industry Forum lobby group asserted the sales clearly triggered a US$11 collapse in the world gold price and a 13 percent decline in Australia's gold equities market, translating into a A$1.6 billion collapse in the value of Australian gold mining companies in the last week.
The fall in price means it will clearly be less economic to mine gold in Australia, Mackay-Coghill said.
"The miners just don't have the funds, so they are going to be fighting to survive. There will not be the funds for exploration expenditure," he said.
Gold Corp refines about 166 tonnes of gold annually, mostly from Australia, the world's number three producer with an annual yield approaching 300 tonnes.

Mackay-Coghill said 25 of Australia's medium to large size producers are operating below total average costs, which means "a hell of a lot of gold is going to stay in the ground," affecting refining profits, Mackay-Coghill said.
Last year it cost on average A$460 an ounce to mine gold in Australia, Mackay-Coghill said. Gold currently only fetches about A$430 an ounce.
Gold Corp and its Australian rivals charge a premium of a fixed percentage premium for gold bullion coin above the going gold price, tying profits closely to the market.
Margins are further compounded by the Australian-U.S.dollar exchange rate as gold is priced in U.S. dollars internationally but in domestic terms in Australia.
The relatively strong Australian dollar at the moment means producers and refiners get less local currency for gold.

"If we take the one-ounce coin, which we sell at a three percent premium -- three percent of four hundred dollars is 12 bucks, but three percent of three hundred bucks is nine bucks -- that's a huge difference in an area where the margins are very tight," Mackay-Coghill said.

Gold Corp is one of three refineries in Australia, each relying on margins derived mainly from upgrading the value of the precious metal for the jewellery, industrial and other markets for profits. The other refineries are Golden West Refining Corp Ltd and Johnson Matthey Plc
"The only way refineries in Australia today make any money is by value-adding to the gold," Mackay-Coghill said.
"Refining on itself... the costs are so low that you can't make money," he said.

Mackay-Coghill said there was no question that Australian gold miners that are less insulated from day-to-day prices by forward hedge sales would be more exposed to foreign takeovers because of a hobbled gold price.
Gold was fixed in London earlier this week at its lowest in 12 years as investors walked away from gold after Australia said it had turned seller.
The possibility of higher foreign ownership of Australian gold mines weakens the RBA's argument against high reserves given the large "in-ground" reserves of Australia.
"Gold in the ground that is uneconomic to mine is not a reserve," he said. Moreover "as long as assets in the ground belong to foreign companies they are not assets to the Reserve Bank," he said.
Mackay-Coghill said it was difficult to square the RBA sales with national economic gain.
"There's no question they did not understand what the were doing," he said.
The amount of gold currently being sold forward in derivative markets is so high that in a declining market the majority of investors hold short positions.
"What you've got is a couple of hundred tonnes of gold sold short, so the leverage in the derivatives markets is such that the dollars in that dwarf whatever the physical gold sales are," he said.
Longer-term fundamentals pointing to high consumption should come back into play, though, he added.
